question: Which of the following best describes an oscillatory (vibratory) motion?
options: A to-and-fro motion about an equilibrium position inside the path, where a restoring force returns the body towards that position
Any motion that repeats in exactly the same way without an equilibrium position
Uniform motion in a straight line
Motion whose acceleration is constant in time
explanation: In oscillatory motion the body has an equilibrium position within its path; there is no net force there, and a small displacement brings a restoring force that drives it back. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but every periodic motion need not be oscillatory (e.g. uniform circular motion).

question: A motion that repeats itself at regular intervals of time is called:
explanation: Periodic motion repeats itself at regular intervals of time — the insect on the ramp, the child on the step and the bouncing ball are examples (Fig 13.1). Oscillatory motion is a special case of periodic motion about an equilibrium position.

question: The human heart beats about 75 times per minute. Its frequency of beating is:
explanation: Frequency is beats per second: f = 75/60 = 1.25 s⁻¹ = 1.25 Hz. The reciprocal gives the time between beats, the period.

question: The period of the heartbeat that beats 75 times per minute is:
explanation: T = 1/f = 1/1.25 = 0.8 s. Note 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹, so a frequency of 1.25 Hz gives one beat every 0.8 seconds.

question: The hertz (Hz), the SI unit of frequency, is defined as:
explanation: By definition 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second = 1 s⁻¹. The unit is named after Heinrich Rudolf Hertz (1857–1894). Frequency need not be an integer — it is just 1/T.

question: The period T and frequency ν of a motion are related by:
explanation: After one period the motion repeats, so in one second the motion goes through f cycles — T = 1/f (Eq 13.1). Larger frequency means shorter period, and vice-versa.

question: In this chapter, the 'displacement' of an oscillating system refers to:
options: The change with time of any physical property under consideration — position, angle, voltage, pressure, field, etc.
Only the change in position of the centre of mass
The distance travelled in one period
The path length between two consecutive mean positions
explanation: Displacement is defined broadly: the position of a spring block, the angle of a pendulum from the vertical, the voltage across a capacitor, the pressure in a sound wave, or the electric/magnetic field in a light wave — any physical quantity that varies sinusoidally in time. It may be positive or negative and is a periodic function of time.

question: The simplest periodic function f(t) = A cos ωt repeats itself after a period:
explanation: cos ωt returns to the same value when its argument changes by 2π, i.e. ωT = 2π, giving T = 2π/ω (Eq 13.3b). Then f(t) = f(t + T) for all t. The sine function and linear combinations share the same property.

question: For f(t) = A sin ωt + B cos ωt = D sin(ωt + φ), the amplitude D and phase constant φ satisfy:
options: D = √(A² + B²) and tan φ = B/A
D = A + B and tan φ = A/B
D = √(A² − B²) and tan φ = A/B
explanation: Writing A = D cos φ and B = D sin φ, adding their squares gives D = √(A² + B²) and dividing gives tan φ = B/A. The combination is periodic with the same period T = 2π/ω (Eq 13.3c, 13.3d).

question: Which of the following functions of time is NON-periodic?
explanation: e^(−ωt) decreases monotonically and never repeats, so it is non-periodic (likewise log(ωt), which grows without bound). The sine combinations are periodic: sinωt + cosωt has period 2π/ω, and sinωt + cos2ωt + sin4ωt repeats with the least common period 2π/ω. (Example 13.2.)

question: Simple harmonic motion is defined as motion in which:
options: The displacement from the mean position is a sinusoidal function of time, x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ)
The body moves with uniform speed along a circle
Displacement is inversely proportional to time
The restoring force is proportional to the square of displacement
explanation: SHM is the displacement being a sinusoidal function of time: x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) with constants A, ω, φ (Eq 13.4). SHM is NOT any periodic motion — it is the simplest oscillatory motion.

question: In the SHM x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), the constant A is called the:
options: Amplitude — the magnitude of the maximum displacement
explanation: A is the amplitude, the magnitude of the maximum displacement; the displacement varies between +A and −A. It is taken as a positive constant without loss of generality.

question: In x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), the quantity (ωt + φ) is called the:
options: Phase of the motion — it fixes the position and velocity at time t
explanation: The phase (ωt + φ) determines the state of the particle (position and velocity) at any time t. The constant φ is the phase constant, the value of the phase at t = 0, found from the initial displacement once the amplitude is known.

question: The angular frequency ω of an SHM of period T (SI unit) is:
explanation: Since cos repeats when its argument changes by 2π, the periodicity demands ωT = 2π, so ω = 2π/T = 2πν, with SI unit rad s⁻¹ (Eq 13.7). For the same amplitude and phase constant, a larger ω means a shorter period.

question: The function sin² ωt represents:
options: Periodic motion with period π/ω, but NOT simple harmonic (it oscillates about ½)
SHM of period π/ω with mean position at zero
explanation: sin² ωt = ½ − ½ cos 2ωt: it is harmonic in form but its mean position is at ½ (not zero), so it is periodic with period π/ω but not SHM. (Example 13.3.)

question: A particle moves uniformly (angular speed ω) on a reference circle of radius A. The projection of its position on a diameter is:
options: x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) — simple harmonic motion
x(t) = A ω t — uniform on the diameter
x(t) = A sin(ωt) with amplitude Aω
explanation: If the initial position vector OP makes angle φ with the x-axis, after time t the angle is ωt + φ, so the x-projection is x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) — exactly the defining equation of SHM. This is why the shadow of a ball on a rotating turntable appears to oscillate. The projection on the y-axis gives y = A sin(ωt + φ), the same motion with phase shifted by π/2. (Section 13.4.)

question: For the SHM x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), the velocity at any instant is:
explanation: Differentiating x(t) (or projecting the uniform circular-motion velocity v = ωA, Eq 13.8) gives v = dx/dt = −ωA sin(ωt + φ) (Eq 13.9, 13.10). The negative sign shows v points opposite to the +x direction as the particle returns. Speed is maximum at the mean position and zero at the extremes.

question: In SHM the acceleration is always:
options: Proportional to the displacement and directed opposite to it: a = −ω²x
Proportional to and directed along the displacement
Zero at the extremes and maximum at the mean position
explanation: Differentiating the velocity gives a = −ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x (Eq 13.11). The acceleration is proportional to displacement and always directed towards the mean position (x > 0 ⇒ a < 0); its magnitude is maximum at the extremes and zero at the mean position.

question: Using Newton's second law, the force law for a particle in SHM is:
options: F = −kx with k = mω², always directed towards the mean position
explanation: From F = ma and a = −ω²x one gets F = −mω²x = −kx with k = mω² (Eq 13.13, 13.14a). This is the restoring force: proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position. Conversely, any force of the form −kx (plus Newton's law) defines SHM (Eq 13.14b gives ω = √(k/m)).

question: The time period of a block of mass m attached to a spring of spring constant k oscillating in SHM is:
explanation: With ω = √(k/m) from the force law, T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k). A stiffer spring (larger k) and a lighter block both give a shorter period.

question: Two identical springs, each of constant k, are attached to the two sides of a block of mass m. Displaced by x from the mean position, the net restoring force and period are:
explanation: The left spring is elongated by x, pulling the block back with −kx; the right spring is compressed by x, pushing it back with another −kx. Total F = −2kx, so the system behaves as a single spring of constant 2k: T = 2π√(m/2k). (Example 13.6.)

question: At the extreme positions (x = ±A) of linear SHM, the kinetic energy K of the particle is:
options: Zero, and the potential energy is maximum
Maximum, and the potential energy is zero
explanation: At x = ±A the speed is zero, so K = 0 and the entire energy is stored as potential energy: U = ½kA² (Eq 13.15–13.17). At the mean position (x = 0) all the energy is kinetic; the period of both K and U (each peaking twice) is T/2.

question: The total mechanical energy of a particle executing linear SHM:
options: Is conserved and equal to ½kA² at all times
Oscillates with the same period as the displacement
Depends on time as cos²(ωt + φ)
Is zero at the mean position
explanation: E = U + K = ½kA²[cos²(ωt+φ) + sin²(ωt+φ)] = ½kA², a constant (Eq 13.18). Because the spring force is conservative, the total energy is conserved; kinetic and potential energy simply interchange with each other during the motion.

question: The potential energy of an SHM at displacement x from the mean position is:
explanation: For the conservative spring force U = ½kx² (Eq 13.16), giving U = ½kA² cos²(ωt + φ) with the displacement law (Eq 13.17). It is zero at the mean position, maximum at the extremes, and periodic with period T/2. The undetermined additive constant is chosen so that U = 0 at x = 0.

question: For a simple pendulum (small bob on a massless, inextensible string of length L) oscillating through small angles, the period is:
explanation: For a massless string the moment of inertia is I = mL², so T = 2π√(I/mgL) reduces to T = 2π√(L/g) (Eq 13.25, 13.26) — independent of the mass of the bob. This holds only for small oscillations, where sin θ ≈ θ (Table 13.1).

question: A seconds pendulum has a period of exactly 2 s. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², its length is approximately:
explanation: From L = gT²/4π² = 9.8 × 4/(4π²) ≈ 1 m (Example 13.8). A pendulum one metre long beats seconds on Earth.

question: A block of mass 3 kg is attached to a spring of spring constant 1200 N m⁻¹, pulled down by 2.0 cm and released. Calculate (i) the frequency of oscillation, (ii) the maximum acceleration, and (iii) the maximum speed of the block.
answer: (i) ω = √(k/m) = √(1200/3) = √400 = 20 rad s⁻¹, so ν = ω/2π = 20/2π ≈ 3.18 Hz. (ii) a_max = ω²A = (20)² × (0.02) = 8 m s⁻² (equivalently kA/m = 1200 × 0.02/3). (iii) v_max = ωA = 20 × 0.02 = 0.40 m s⁻¹. Answers: (i) 3.18 Hz, (ii) 8 m s⁻², (iii) 0.40 m s⁻¹.
explanation: The frequency depends only on √(k/m); the maximum acceleration occurs at the extreme displacement where a = −ω²x, and the maximum speed occurs at the mean position, v_max = ωA. Use metres for amplitude (2.0 cm = 0.02 m). (Exercise 13.9.)

question: A particle executes SHM with amplitude 4 cm. At a displacement of 2 cm its acceleration is 8 cm s⁻². Determine the time period of the motion and the maximum speed of the particle.
answer: Using a = −ω²x in magnitude: ω² = a/x = 8/2 = 4, so ω = 2 rad s⁻¹. Period T = 2π/ω = π s ≈ 3.14 s. Maximum speed v_max = ωA = 2 × 4 = 8 cm s⁻¹. Answers: T = π s and v_max = 8 cm s⁻¹.
explanation: The SHM acceleration is a = −ω²x, so measuring a and x at any instant fixes ω without needing the mass or spring constant. Then T = 2π/ω and v_max = ωA follow directly.
